skills.when_to_use: Use when the question demands precise cross-video correspondence, discrimination, or selection among videos/options, recognizable from the question text and video list alone: questions that reference labeled object IDs across synchronized camera views and ask where an object is, how it moves or where it ends up, or whether it is visible when an event involving another object occurs; questions that name a time interval or timestamp in one video and ask for the functionally equivalent step or interval in another, or otherwise require a time-interval answer about a specific visible action; questions asking which of several videos, segments, or options exhibits a stated property, state, error, or ending condition; or questions asking which action is performed incorrectly a stated number of times across videos of the same activity. Do not use for open narrative inference questions (e.g., predicting a middle segment from a beginning and an ending) where summarizing each video separately suffices.
skills.strategy: Apply this procedure in order; it overrides the default single-pass workflow. Stage 1, neutral first acquisition: for each referenced video, issue one per-video instruction asking for a timestamped, purely descriptive account of the relevant objects, actions, or scenes — every occurrence with its visible start and end seconds and visible attributes — plus a complete timeline of all occurrences of the target action across the whole video, not just the first instance found. Do not embed the answer options, a yes/no verdict request, or an expected conclusion in the first pass: verdict-seeking instructions bias the analyst toward confirming or denying the premise instead of reporting what is visible. For a property-selection question (which video shows, ends with, or contains X), ask each video for a raw description of the relevant moments (who and what is present, positions, objects held, visible threats or errors) and decide the property yourself from those raw details, never from the analyst's own verdict. For a referenced event at a stated time, request that interval plus several seconds of surrounding context. Stage 2, mandatory flags before answering — check every accumulated report and raise a flag when: (a) two reports about the same object or moment directly conflict, including a later report that locates something an earlier report called not visible or unidentifiable; (b) a question-referenced labeled object, or the conditioning event the question depends on, is reported not visible or unidentifiable by a single-video agent — absence in one report is not evidence of absence; (c) a degenerate time appears: any candidate moment anchored at 0.0 seconds or at a selected clip's start boundary; any interval whose two bounds equal the boundaries of a window you previously requested or selected in an earlier call; or a single point where the question requires an interval with distinct start and end; (d) a report's raw visual description contradicts its own interpretive conclusion (e.g., a weapon at a character's neck is described but the summary concludes no danger); (e) a candidate interval came from a joint watch whose total selected duration was long relative to the detail sought, so sampling was too sparse to localize a brief action reliably; (f) the best raw observation matches none of the answer options. Stage 3, resolve every flag with one focused follow-up; never answer from flagged evidence and never guess from assumptions about how such question sets are usually constructed. For a not-visible or unidentifiable labeled object, or an identity/position conflict across synchronized views, run a joint watch of the relevant views naming the video IDs, asking the visual model to locate each labeled object using its first-second colored box and describe the raw visual layout and movement at the relevant moment, without stating which answer option is correct; keep the total selected duration small so sampling stays dense enough for brief or fine-grained events. For any time-interval answer, before submitting it run one dense confirmation watch on a tight window covering the candidate interval plus a few seconds before and after, asking for the action's full visible start and end seconds, how long it visibly continues after it begins, and whether the same action occurs at any other time; adjust or reject the candidate interval according to this confirmation, and never submit an interval identical to a previously requested or selected window without it. For an anchor claimed at 0.0 seconds or at a clip boundary, densely re-watch the first several seconds and any later candidate moments before accepting it. When a raw observation matches none of the options, re-verify that moment with a dense re-watch before reinterpreting it; do not infer 'not visible' by eliminating the other options. Stage 4, final answer from raw description: answer only from the described visual content, not from an analyst's or visual model's verdict phrase and not from plausibility priors about intended answers. Never encode an unresolved observation as an observed state — for example, do not answer 'stay in place' or 'not visible' merely because a labeled object could not be found; that is unresolved evidence requiring Stage 3, and if it remains unresolved after the follow-up, choose the option whose support rests on the strongest described visual details, re-read the raw descriptions for a detail that resolves the choice, and record the residual uncertainty in the answer's reason. Never substitute a discussion of missing evidence for the requested answer representation.
